caption:
What does ‘glass skin’ actually mean? It is a visual beauty ideal—not a medical diagnosis.

Lighting, makeup, facial oil, hydration, texture, and editing can all change the glossy finish you see online. If shine comes with burning, tightness, or persistent redness, stop adding products, simplify the routine, and seek care if it persists or worsens.

In Korean skincare, a better goal is comfortable, stable skin with real texture. Save this before adding another step.

General education only.

first_comment: How many steps are in your routine right now? And if you had to remove one tomorrow, which one goes first? Curious whether the answer is the newest step or the oldest one.

slides.alt_text: Slide 1 of 6: A glass pane and a rose quartz gua sha stone in bright light. Title: Glass skin should not burn to look glossy.
Slide 2 of 6: Three cream circles like highlights on dark green. Light, oil, makeup and editing can create shine in seconds.
Slide 3 of 6: Three cards for healthy-looking glow: comfort with no burning, a routine you tolerate, and real texture.
Slide 4 of 6: Three outlined triangles labelled burning, tightness and redness — signs of irritation, not of purging.
Slide 5 of 6: Five stacked bars: cleanse, tone, serum, mask, procedure. Every extra step is harder to troubleshoot.
Slide 6 of 6: Three cards: no burning, no chasing shine, still human texture. Save this before adding another step.
